title: “It’s a form of survival”: Autistic transgender and nonbinary people’s experiences of disordered eating
description:
Autistic transgender and/or nonbinary (TNB) people are a multiply marginalised group systematically impacted by high rates of disordered eating. Feminist scholarship has examined the role of systems of oppression in creating environments where disordered eating can flourish, particularly sexism, racism and weight stigma. We expand this conversation by taking an intersectional, minority stress lens to examine the roles of cis-heteronormativity and neuronormativity in disordered eating in Autistic TNB people. Twenty-one Autistic TNB participants (aged 19-51) with disordered eating were asked to take part in narrative online interviews that were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. 
Participants framed their disordered eating as a survival technique. In line with minority stress theory, disordered eating was articulated both as a direct response to systemic and interpersonal violence, and an indirect response to internalisation of queerphobic or anti-Autistic experiences. A struggle for belonging characterised participants’ intersectional experience. Queer communities provided a site of acceptance and improved disordered eating for some, yet were also places that could exacerbate unbelonging and disordered eating through intersecting ableism, racism and fatphobia and the communication of queer-specific appearance pressures. 
Findings demonstrate the utility of an intersectional minority stress lens to examine Autistic TNB health inequities. Beyond individualised neuro- and gender-affirming approaches for Autistic TNB people with disordered eating, researchers and clinicians must move towards an emancipatory approach which considers the systemic factors influencing the mental health of this multiple minoritised community.

title: “ChatGPT Is My Best Friend”: AI as an Ambivalent Source of Social Support in Reddit Mental Health Communities
description: As artificial intelligence (AI) enters everyday mental health communication, people increasingly turn to chatbots for reassurance, advice, and companionship. Drawing on Social Support Theory and the Computers Are Social Actors (CASA) framework, this study examined how members of ten Reddit mental health communities discuss AI in relation to mental health. We analyzed 10,042 AI-related posts, modeled their themes with structural topic modeling, measured affective language with LIWC, and estimated engagement with negative binomial models across the period surrounding ChatGPT's launch. We found thirteen themes covering every functional category of support that users sought from AI, positioning it as an informational aid, productivity assistant, therapist substitute, and companion, and also as a threat. Discussion shifted from tool-oriented uses toward clinically salient, emotionally charged themes, and its tone grew gradually more negative and anxious after the launch, diverging from a matched non-AI baseline from the same communities. Therapy-substitute and existential-threat themes drew the most engagement, whereas prevalent comfort-seeking drew little. Theoretically, the study extends social support theory by casting a nonhuman actor as a source users enlist across emotional, appraisal, informational, and instrumental functions yet also appraise as a threat, and it draws on CASA to interpret when people grant or withhold social standing to a machine. Practically, the findings inform the design and governance of AI tools already used for coping and crisis moments and highlight vulnerable users who rely on AI for private comfort yet remain least visible in peer communities. Findings position AI as an ambivalent, increasingly embedded source of support.

title: Automated Classification of Restrictive and Repetitive Behaviors in Autistic Children
description: Restricted and repetitive behaviors (RRBs) are a common class of behavior in autistic children, and their assessment is typically based on presence and severity. While previous research has primarily focused on detecting RRBs (i.e., presence or type), automated classification of severity levels has received limited attention. The present study aimed to categorize RRB severity in 58 autistic children using clinician-labeled data based on the Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule (ADOS). A machine learning model was evaluated under two strategies: session-based and participant-based analyses. The model achieved high accuracy for session-based training (Cohen’s kappa = 0.82) whereas accuracy decreased for participant-based training (Cohen’s kappa = 0.54), indicating reduced generalization to new children. Confusion matrix analysis showed clearer class separation in the session-based analysis and greater overlap among ratings in the participant-based analysis. These findings suggest that the automated rating of RRBs is feasible, but that inter-individual variability remains a challenge for participant-independent applications.

title: Methodological Consistency and Measurement Standards in Mindfulness-Based Randomized Controlled Trials for Racial Minorities: A Systematic Review
description: Mindfulness-based interventions (MBIs) are increasingly delivered to racial minority populations, yet the methodological rigor and measurement practices underlying this literature have not been systematically evaluated. Following PRISMA guidelines, this review examined 20 U.S. randomized controlled trials (RCTs) of MBIs with samples of at least 75% racial minority participants. Each study was coded for location, adaptation type, MBI framework, control condition, solo practice, practice style, and outcome measure, and assessed for quality using modified Jadad criteria. Studies were additionally rated with the Hall et al. Mindfulness Methods Score, a novel tool developed from prior methodological recommendations. Scores ranged from 4 to 6 out of a possible 7. Reporting of intervention delivery was a consistent strength: all 20 studies described or linked their protocols, 19 described the intervention teachers, and 16 detailed the theory, content, and frequency of the practices used. Studies varied considerably in location, framework, and solo practice requirements, and none tested an un-adapted, standard MBI protocol, leaving no empirical baseline against which adaptations can be evaluated. The most consequential gap, however, concerned mindfulness itself. Eleven of the 20 studies administered no trait or state mindfulness measure, and none used a non-self-report measure. Without direct measurement of the proposed mechanism of change, neither the effect of adaptations nor the risk of adverse response can be evaluated empirically. Future research should administer explicit trait and state mindfulness measures, establish a standard-protocol baseline, and engage the methodological critiques directed at the broader mindfulness literature.

title: Evaluating the Effectiveness of MediLanguage’s Language Support Starter: A Digital Decision Aid to Support the Selection of Communication Strategies to Overcome Language Barriers in General Practice
description:
Objective: Migrant patients with limited proficiency in the host country's dominant language(s) often face difficulties in making informed decisions about selecting communication strategies to overcome language barriers. This study evaluated MediLanguage’s Language Support Starter, an evidence-based digital decision aid developed through the Spiral Technology Action Research Model with migrant patients, usability experts, and healthcare providers, using an iterative process. This approach led to MediLanguage’s Language Support Starter, designed to empower patients to select appropriate communication strategies before language-discordant medical consultations, thereby facilitating shared decision-making with their healthcare providers (HCPs) during these consultations. 
Methods: A cluster-randomised controlled trial (RCT) was conducted in seven Dutch general practices, involving 18 participating HCPs and 75 Turkish-Dutch patients (31 in the control group and 44 in the intervention group; Mage = 61.79, SD = 12.40), all of whom had limited proficiency in Dutch. While questionnaires assessing HCPs’ demographics and perceived communication self-efficacy were administered once before the start of the trial, questionnaires were given to patients both before and after consultations. Control patients received standard care; intervention patients used MediLanguage’s Language Support Starter prior to their consultations. 
Results: There were no differences between HCPs in the intervention and control groups regarding their perceived communication self-efficacy. On a scale from 1 to 10, they scored an average of 7.30 (SD = 1.23), indicating a high level of confidence in their ability to communicate with Turkish-Dutch patients with limited Dutch language proficiency. MediLanguage was well received for its ease of use, comprehensiveness, and attractiveness to patients. title: Affective Valence and Temporal Framing: A Unified Generative Model of the Temporal Structure of Emotion
description: Emotions are temporally structured: regret concerns what has happened, anxiety what will happen, joy what is happening now. Three strands of the active-inference literature each formalise one temporal face of affect: backward valence as the negative rate of change of variational free energy (Joffily and Coricelli 2013), present valence as reward prediction error (Pattisapu et al. 2025), and forward valence as the affective charge of policy revision (Hesp et al. 2021). Yet none alone spans the full temporal range, unifies these quantities into a taxonomy of emotion, or models how an agent actively selects the temporal orientation that dominates its own affect. We develop a single factored generative model in which a hidden temporal-frame state (past/present/future) redistributes precision across horizons, so that framing emerges from expected-free-energy minimisation. We motivate the architecture from the psychology of mental time travel, understood as the graded, cost-bounded regulation of how deeply memories and plans are unrolled, and show that a single depth regulator with two temporal faces reproduces the classical split between rumination (past-directed) and worry (future-directed). Affect here is a readout layer over a task-specific generative model, and the three channels are general operators on its inference dynamics. Driven by real experience-sampling sequences, the full model predicts next-moment affect out of sample better than linear autoregressive baselines, roughly doubling one-step skill where affect is volatile (held-out R² = 0.19 vs 0.09); the lead replicates in an independent second sample. title: Disentangling Negative Affectivity and General Psychopathology in Early Childhood: A Multi-Trait Multi-Method Approach to Validity and Informant Perspectives
description:
Background
Children’s emotional and behavioral problems frequently co-occur, suggesting the existence of a general factor of psychopathology ("p factor") that accounts for the shared variance across internalizing and externalizing problems. Ongoing questions remain regarding the extent to which negative affectivity—a temperamental tendency to display observable manifestations likely reflecting negative emotions—and general psychopathology represent overlapping versus distinct constructs across early development. 

Methods
A community-based sample of 231 children aged 3 to 7 years participated in an accelerated longitudinal study, with assessments at four timepoints spaced nine months apart. Data were collected via multi-informant (mother, father, teacher/secondary caregiver) ratings, structured observational tasks, and standard questionnaires. This study evaluated the convergent and discriminant validity of negative affectivity and general psychopathology measures across informants and methods using multitrait-multimethod matrices while accounting for the unique perspective of the informant.

Results
Findings indicated that measures of negative affectivity and general psychopathology exhibited moderate convergent validity but also retained distinctiveness, supporting the discriminant validity in measures of these constructs. The association between the two was somewhat attenuated when controlling for informant type.

Conclusions
The results clarify that, although negative affectivity and general psychopathology are closely related in childhood, they are not redundant constructs. Additionally, the observed deflation in the association between negative affectivity and general psychopathology after accounting for the unique perspective of the informant highlights how measurement strategies—including informant source and method variance—can meaningfully alter interpretations of the associations between psychopathology and risk/protective factors. title: (Computation of) the Standardized Mean Difference in Clinical Trials Should be Standardized
description: The standardized mean difference (SMD) is widely used in psychology clinical trials to convert intervention effect estimates from raw units to a common scale, enabling comparison across settings. However, multiple operationalizations of the SMD are possible for clinical trial data, with large potential impacts on estimate magnitudes. In this commentary, I review practices for operationalizing the SMD in the Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology and other journals that publish results of clinical trials. I find that only one-third of studies report sufficient information to determine the operationalization. Among those, the operationalization varies widely, threatening the SMD’s utility in providing a common scale. Given the common goals and design elements across many trials, it is feasible to establish a default operationalization for the SMD’s standardizer. I outline eight desirable SMD properties and evaluate each option against these properties. The pooled baseline standard deviation meets seven of eight, far more than any alternative, with its main limitation being susceptibility to inflation from restrictive inclusion criteria. I conclude that raw effect estimates should be divided by the pooled baseline standard deviation as a default, one-size-fits-most choice. Adopting this standard will help the SMD meet its promise as a standardized metric, improving comparability of results across different measures, outcomes, studies, and populations. I also provide reporting recommendations to improve transparency and enable re-computation using alternative standardizers when needed.

title: The Dynamic Hierarchy of Personal Space Regulation and its Modulation by Childhood Traumatic Experiences
description: Personal space (PS) regulation represents a core component of socio-affective functioning, requiring the dynamic coordination of perception, affect, and behavior. Yet how these components are hierarchically organized and how adverse childhood experiences modulate this organization remain unclear. To address these gaps, 57 healthy participants underwent a computerized audiovisual stop-distance paradigm. Participants were presented with social (angry, neutral faces) and non-social (ball) stimuli approaching at two speeds. Across trials, participants stopped the stimulus at their preferred distance and rated perceived distance, perceived speed, discomfort, and threat. Bayesian multilevel modeling revealed a hierarchical Perception→Affect→Behavior architecture sustained by two functionally distinct pathways: a spatial–behavioral pathway in which perceived distance directly predicted interpersonal distance, and a temporal–affective pathway in which perceived speed predicted behavior primarily through affective elaboration. Childhood trauma was quantified using the Childhood Trauma Questionnaire (CTQ) as a continuous measure. First, higher CTQ scores were associated with broader interpersonal distances across conditions and with amplified perceptual-affective reactivity to fast approach dynamics. Second, childhood trauma selectively restructured the spatial–behavioral pathway when stimuli were perceived as distant, shifting regulation from bodily discomfort toward anticipatory threat evaluation, while the temporal–affective pathway remained preserved. Third, higher childhood trauma scores were associated with reduced habituation of affective and behavioral responses across repeated trials. These findings characterize PS as a hierarchical dynamic regulatory system in which spatial and temporal cues engage distinct functional routes. title: Investigating the longevity of real-world memory following a smartphone intervention in older adults: A multi-year follow-up study
description: Our ability to recollect details from personal past events tends to decline with age, which can affect how we act in the world, communicate with others, and understand ourselves. HippoCamera is a neuroscience-guided smartphone application that aims to mitigate these age-related memory changes by guiding users to record and review cues for real-world events using established mnemonic strategies. Previous work demonstrated improved episodic recollection and enhanced hippocampal activity for events reviewed using HippoCamera. Here, we followed up with 25 older adults 3.5 to 6 years after their participation in a HippoCamera study, using a mixed-methods approach to assess the longevity of these memory benefits. Participants reported greater subjective re-experiencing for events that were previously reviewed using HippoCamera relative to events that were only recorded but never reviewed. Further, participants reported greater subjective re-experiencing for events recorded using HippoCamera compared to events that were cued with calendar entries from a comparable time period. Using semi-structured interviews, we also explored the experience of using HippoCamera itself and reminiscing upon their past recorded events. Participants spoke to the benefits of HippoCamera not only for episodic memory, but more broadly to their daily lifestyle and activities, and their sense of meaning and well-being. Participants also reflected upon their attitudes and beliefs both towards HippoCamera and their own memory as it changes with age. Altogether, these results demonstrate the broad and long-lasting effects of a smartphone-based tool that improves memory for real-world events and enriches how older adults relate to their own past experiences.

title: Difficult conversations as Self-Control Conflicts
description: Why do people avoid having important but difficult conversations? The dominant explanation is that people are overly pessimistic about the outcomes of conversations— overestimating costs and underestimating benefits. However, anecdotal evidence suggests people still fail to initiate conversations they expect to be more beneficial than costly. We address this puzzle by testing a self-control account of difficult conversations. Like other classic self-control conflicts (e.g., going to the gym, eating healthily), we argue that engaging in difficult conversations requires people to overcome proximal, concrete costs (e.g., feeling uncomfortable, hurting someone’s feelings in the moment) in pursuit of distal, abstract benefits (e.g., helping someone grow). Across four pilot studies and six experiments (N = 2,442), we provide three key pieces of support for our account. First, people perceive difficult conversations as having intertemporal trade-offs, such that the costs precede the benefits. Second, people’s decisions to initiate difficult conversations are sensitive to time, such that people are more willing to have difficult conversations in the future than the present (i.e., they delay). Importantly, this effect is specific to conversations that are expected to have both costs and benefits, suggesting that people do not generally delay all conversations. This delay is mediated by differential weighing of the costs and benefits in addition to lower anticipated costs in the future (vs. the present). Third, people are more willing to take up costly commitment devices to motivate themselves to initiate difficult conversations than to take up equivalently costly gambles. This suggests that people are aware of these dynamics. Overall, we provide a new theoretical lens for understanding difficult conversations and point to new interventions to prompt them.

title: Closed-book and open-book language model assessment  of employee experience.  A two-sample convergent validity study comparing  multi-stage retrieval and single-prompt approaches
description: Language models are increasingly used to produce quantitative judgements about organisations from publicly available text, yet such systems differ fundamentally in whether they consult external evidence at the point of judgement or draw only on knowledge encoded during training. This study compared two systems that estimate the same 24 dimensions of employee experience using the same base language model and differ only in how evidence is gathered: a multi-stage retrieval approach, assembling each score through staged web retrieval and sequential scoring over two to three hours per organisation, and a single-prompt approach, producing all dimensions in one call from parametric knowledge. Because the two share a base model, the comparison isolates the contribution of retrieval. Evidence came from two independent samples, comprising 35 large, well-known companies and 152 organisations spanning insurance, retail, healthcare, education and professional services. Both approaches proved reliable across repeated runs (ICC(A,1) = .84 to .97). Convergence between them was moderate, with per-dimension correlations averaging .79 and .63 in the two samples and rising to .81 and .72 after correction for attenuation, and was consistently stronger for an organisation's overall score than for individual dimensions (corrected r = .91 and .85). Performance varied systematically by dimension in both samples: agreement was highest on dimensions describing an organisation's public identity, such as brand, mission and rewards, and lowest on those describing internal working experience, such as the direct manager, career progression, and diversity and inclusion. Retrieval contributed most where public text carries least, suggesting that gathering evidence determines which parts of a construct can be measured rather than simply improving accuracy.

title: Turn-Duration Burstiness as a Temporal Signature of Collective Cognitive Demand in Multidisciplinary Healthcare Team Meetings
description: Collective cognition in team settings is shaped not only by what is communicated, but by the temporal dynamics of how communication unfolds. Multidisciplinary team meetings (MDTMs) in oncological care offer a naturalistic window into collective decision-making under real-world constraints, where teams of medical clinicians must jointly process complex patient cases. In this study, we examine the temporal structure of speech turn durations in oncological MDTMs using burstiness, a measure of how irregularly communication is distributed over time, as a quantitative index of communicative temporal organization. We applied two complementary burstiness metrics, the burstiness parameter (B) and the length-normalized variant (Aₙ(r)), to meeting and case-level speech turn data, and used random intercept models to examine associations between burstiness, case complexity, and case processing time. Communication was predominantly bursty, exceeding levels expected under a random process. More complex cases were associated with higher burstiness, suggesting that irregular temporal communication structure has potential to serve as an observable marker of collective cognitive load. Growth curve modeling further revealed significant main effects of burstiness and case order on case processing time, as well as interactions moderated by MDT sample. These results indicate that temporal communication dynamics and case processing is context dependent varying systematically across meeting types and as meetings progress. These findings suggest that burstiness may reflect meaningful variation in the collective cognitive dynamics of MDTMs and may offer a promising foundation for real-time monitoring of team interactions and decision-making.

title: Italian Adaptation and Validation of the ICAR-16 Sample Test
description: The International Cognitive Ability Resource 16 (ICAR-16) is a public-domain measure of cognitive ability. However, no Italian validation currently exists. We translated and validated the ICAR-16 in a sample of 486 Italian adults (66% females), who completed the ICAR-16 and the long version of the Cognitive Reflection Test online. Confirmatory factor analyses supported the original hierarchical structure, with the Second-Order Latent Variable model (CFI=.98; TLI=.98) showing the best fit. Moreover, the ICAR-16 correlates strongly with the Cognitive Reflection Test (CRT) (ϕ= .81; 95% CI: .75, .86), confirming convergent validity. Internal consistency reliability was also adequate (ωt = .82; ωh = .59; α= .78). Measurement invariance analyses supported partial scalar invariance across sexes, with no further decrement in fit indexes for strict invariance. Only one item (MR47) exhibited uniform Differential Item Functioning. Overall, these findings support the Italian ICAR-16 as a reliable, freely available instrument for cognitive assessment in research.

title: Self-Efficacy Predicts Differential Neuroticism Change in a Smartphone-Based Intervention
description: Self-guided, digital interventions can help people change their personality traits in desired directions, including becoming less neurotic. However, little is known about how and why people differ in intervention-related changes. Theoretical models state that intentional personality change must be perceived as feasible and that being motivated to change is not sufficient to elicit lasting trait changes. Using a German-speaking sample (N = 446; M_age = 25.88; 85% female; Residence: 47% Switzerland, 26% Germany, 26% Austria, 1% Other), we tested whether self-efficacy and growth mindset predict change in multiple neuroticism measures across a 6-week intervention and 2-month follow-up. To isolate temporal processes during the intervention, we examined co-development of weekly neuroticism and self-efficacy and their week-to-week temporal associations. We found evidence for self-efficacy predicting differential neuroticism change but not for growth mindset. Participants with higher self-efficacy showed greater pre-post decreases in self-reported neuroticism and greater pre-post increases in emotional resilience than those with lower self-efficacy. At follow-up, participants with higher self-efficacy continued to improve more in neuroticism and emotional resilience. Last, higher self-efficacy in one week predicted lower neuroticism in the following week, and vice versa, independent of participants’ overall trajectories. In contrast, there was no consistent evidence for between-person co-development of weekly self-efficacy and neuroticism across the intervention. Findings support theoretical expectations that perceived feasibility is a precondition for neuroticism change and suggest possible reinforcement mechanisms between weekly self-efficacy and neuroticism. We discuss implications for theory and future intervention studies.

title: Empirical Signatures of Choice-Induced Preference Change
description: Choice-induced preference change refers to the tendency for value estimates to differ after a choice relative to before it. Although this phenomenon is robust, the process that generates it remains debated. In this work, we reanalyzed pooled data from two previous studies to identify empirical signatures to serve as benchmarks for candidate process accounts of choice-induced preference change. We focused on three factors that are especially informative for theory: choice difficulty, deliberation time, and the attribute structure of the options. First, we reproduced the well-established finding that the spreading of alternatives is greater for more difficult choices. Second, we showed that its relationship with response time remains after controlling for difficulty, indicating that the relationship with deliberation time is not reducible to initial value difference alone. Third, we found that preference change depends not only on overall value difference but also on how the options differ in terms of their attributes, with stronger effects for choices laden with tradeoffs than for cases of simple dominance. Together, these results indicate that choice-induced preference change is tied to deliberation itself rather than to a post hoc or artifactual revision of fixed values. The findings are compatible with both value-refinement and coherence-based reasoning accounts in some respects, but they also constrain both by showing that preference change depends jointly on difficulty, deliberation time, and attribute structure.

title: The Morality-Effectiveness Disconnect of Pro-environmental Behaviors
description: Not all pro-environmental behaviors are created equal—some are vastly more effective at mitigating climate change than others. Do people judge the more effective behaviors as proportionally more moral? Five main and six supplemental studies (N = 9,247) across five countries reveal a robust morality-effectiveness disconnect: pro-environmental behaviors that rank better on objective climate-mitigation potential rank worse on individual moral judgments. Laypeople fail to predict this pattern, believing that a positive relationship exists. Further, labeling behaviors by climate impact category reduces the morality-effectiveness disconnect, and detailed impact information reverses it and increases policy endorsement of more effective behaviors over less effective behaviors. While the disconnect primarily stems from effectiveness misperceptions that accurate information can mitigate, we find that personal support for less effective behaviors plays an additional role. Thus, people's moral intuition for climate action appears miscalibrated: moral cognition can undermine the collective welfare that such cognition should presumably promote.

title: Assessment of food cravings and food addiction
description: This chapter briefly defines the terms food craving and food addiction and describes the most common assessment methods. These include self-report instruments such as the Food Cravings Questionnaires, the Food Craving Inventory, the Craving Experience Questionnaire, and the Yale Food Addiction Scale as well as interview measures such as the Food Addiction Symptom Inventory. It concludes by highlighting the overlaps between food craving measures and measures of food addiction as well as related constructs.

title: Reading Tiramisu in Czech and English: Robust Processing Speed Differences in Translation Equivalent Stimuli
description: Cross-linguistic studies of reading have documented broad similarities across languages, yet the extent to which first-language (L1) reading processes differ once structural confounds are minimized remains unclear. We conducted self-paced reading experiments in English and Czech using tightly aligned translation-equivalent sentences, enabling a direct comparison of L1 reading under parallel input conditions. Matched groups of English and Czech L1 speakers (N = 176 per language) showed near-identical comprehension accuracy but robust differences in processing speed: reaction times (RTs) were reliably faster in English than in Czech, a pattern that persisted after controlling for word length and surprisal. At the same time, the effects of classical predictors such as length and surprisal were directionally similar across languages, consistent with universal reading mechanisms. Our analyses suggest two complementary explanations for the observed cross‑linguistic differences. First, Czech exhibits higher information density than English, which—under conditions that prevent skipping and regressions—manifests as slower per‑word reading. Second, surprisal was distributed differently across the two languages: in Czech, surprisal was markedly higher at sentence onset and decreased more steeply over word position, amplifying early‑sentence processing demands. These findings indicate that while core reading processes are universal, language‑specific typological properties shape how information is packaged and distributed across the sentence, yielding systematic cross‑linguistic differences in processing speed. The results parallel cross-linguistic findings on speech rate and support an emerging framework in which reading adapts to the informational structure of the language being processed.

title: Toward a Unified Perspective on Content Analysis
description: Content analysis, the practice of inferring individual difference characteristics from text data, is an important research technique across the behavioral and social sciences. The methods used to conduct it, however, are strikingly heterogenous, reflecting three distinct approaches: human-centered, dictionary-centered, and machine-learning centered. Currently, the utility of content analysis is hindered by a lack of clarity regarding how reliable, valid, and generalizable the outputs from each of these approaches are. This paper examines a cross-section of research on each approach to content analysis, evaluating each approach from the perspective of psychological measurement. Drawing on classical test theory, generalizability theory, latent variable theory, and cognitive psychometrics, I identify some potential sources of variance that shape content-analytic results. I then investigate the reliability of each approach and offer practical recommendations for future research concerning the specific situations where each approach is most appropriate. This paper suggests that the field would benefit from more theoretical cross-fertilization across camps of content analytic research practice, as well as additional work investigating the measurement processes involved in content analysis more generally. It also consolidates the essential elements of different styles of content analytic research practice and sheds light on content analysis’s strengths and limitations.
